title: Effect of heat input and filler metal strength on the HAZ softening and static bending behavior of GMAW-welded connections in Strenx®700MC high-strength steel
abstract: Abstract The influence of heat input on heat-affected zone (HAZ) degradation and structural performance of thermo-mechanically controlled processed (TMCP) high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels remains insufficiently understood, particularly in welded square hollow section (SHS) connections. This study investigates the static bending behavior of gas metal arc welded (GMAW) SHS column-to-beam connections manufactured from Strenx®700MC steel. Undermatching (AWS ER80S-G) and overmatching (AWS ER120S-G) filler metal were employed, and twelve full-scale joints were produced using heat inputs ranging from 0.3 to 1.6 kJ/mm. Experimental bending tests, hardness measurements, analytical calculations, finite element simulations, and two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to evaluate the effects of heat input and filler metal strength on joint performance. Increasing heat input initially improved bending resistance by enhancing weld penetration and effective weld area. However, excessive heat input promoted thermal-cycle-induced HAZ softening, leading to strain localization and reduced load-carrying capacity. An optimal heat input of approximately 1.2 kJ/mm was identified. Although the overmatching filler metal increased nominal weld metal (WM) tensile strength by approximately 44%, the ultimate bending load increased by only 3%, demonstrating a limited structural benefit. Finite element analyses indicated that the highest stress and strain concentrations occurred at the weld toe and adjacent regions where failure initiation was experimentally observed, while two-way ANOVA confirmed that heat input was the dominant factor governing HAZ hardness. The results demonstrate that controlling welding thermal cycles is more effective than increasing filler metal strength for improving the bending performance of welded SHS connections manufactured from TMCP high-strength steels. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The increasing demand for lightweight, energy-efficient, and high-performance structural systems has driven the widespread adoption of TMCP HSLA steels in civil, offshore, and industrial applications [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. These steels offer an attractive combination of high strength, good ductility, and improved weldability, achieved through controlled rolling and accelerated cooling that promote fine-grained microstructures strengthened by precipitation and grain refinement [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]. Among them, Strenx®700MC steels have been extensively employed in structural components where high load-bearing capacity and reduced material usage are required [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ].

Despite their favorable properties, TMCP HSLA steels are inherently sensitive to welding thermal cycles [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. Welding disrupts the carefully engineered process-structure balance established during thermomechanical processing, particularly in the HAZ, where localized microstructural transformations may significantly degrade mechanical properties [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]. As a result, the performance of welded joints in TMCP steels is often governed not by the base metal strength, but by thermal-cycle-induced property gradients that influence stress redistribution, plastic strain localization, and damage development [ 5 ,  17 ,  18 ].

Gas metal arc welding (GMAW) remains one of the most widely used joining processes for TMCP steels due to its versatility and industrial applicability [ 10 ,  11 ]. Among the welding parameters, heat input plays a central role, simultaneously influencing weld geometry, penetration, cooling rate and microstructural evolution in the WM and HAZ [ 19 ,  20 ,  21 – 22 ]. Previous studies have shown that increasing heat input can enhance joint efficiency by improving weld penetration and fusion [ 12 ,  23 ,  24 ]. However, excessive heat input may promote HAZ softening through the coarsening and partial dissolution of Nb(C,N), TiN, and V(C,N) precipitates formed during thermomechanical controlled processing, together with recovery of the deformed ferritic microstructure and localized grain coarsening [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. These transformations reduce precipitation and grain-boundary strengthening, resulting in lower hardness and strength within the HAZ. Consequently, an optimal heat input window is required to balance geometric efficiency and metallurgical integrity [ 7 ,  13 ].

Another critical aspect in the welding of high-strength steels is filler metal mechanical strength mismatch [ 10 ,  19 ,  25 ,  26 ]. Overmatching filler metals are frequently recommended to ensure sufficient joint strength and prevent premature failure in the WM [ 7 ,  10 ]. However, in TMCP steels, the benefits of increasing nominal filler metal tensile strength overmatching may be limited when thermal-cycle-induced HAZ softening becomes the dominant failure-controlling mechanism. Experimental and numerical investigations have increasingly demonstrated that, under bending or constraint-dominated loading conditions, failure frequently initiates in the HAZ or adjacent base metal regions, where local softening and stress concentration dominate the mechanical response [ 7 ,  17 ,  27 ,  28 – 29 ].

Although the effects of heat input and filler metal strength mismatch on high-strength steel joints have been extensively investigated, most available studies address these parameters in an isolated manner. Previous works [ 10 ,  17 ,  30 ] typically focus either on the influence of heat input on microstructural evolution and HAZ softening, or on the mechanical implications of filler metal mismatch, often based on coupon-level tests or simplified joint configurations. Consequently, the combined and interacting effects of thermal cycles and filler metal strength mismatch on the structural-scale performance of welded connections remain insufficiently understood.

In particular, there is a lack of integrated studies conducted at the structural scale that explicitly correlate heat input with thermal-cycle severity, microstructural degradation and hardness gradients in the HAZ, stress redistribution mechanisms, and ultimate load-carrying capacity. This gap is particularly relevant for SHS column-to-beam connections fabricated from TMCP HSLA steels, where the present results suggest that failure initiation under bending-dominated loading is more strongly influenced by thermal-cycle-induced property gradients within the HAZ than by WM strength alone.

Therefore, the present study investigates the process-structure-performance relationships governing the static bending behavior of full-scale GMAW-welded SHS connections manufactured from Strenx®700MC high-strength steel. Special emphasis is placed on quantifying the relative contributions of heat input and filler metal strength mismatch to joint performance. By combining experimental testing, analytical modeling, and numerical simulations, this work suggests that HAZ softening plays a dominant role in controlling the ultimate bending response. In this context, the study explicitly examines whether substantial increases in nominal filler metal tensile strength translate into meaningful structural benefits at the joint level. The working hypothesis of this study is that, for TMCP high-strength steels subjected to bending-dominated loading, thermal-cycle-induced degradation in the HAZ exerts a greater influence on structural performance than WM overmatching.

sections.heading: Materials, welding procedures, and experimental program
Joint design and welding procedure
paragraphs: The SHS joints were welded using the gas metal arc welding (GMAW) process in the flat position with direct current electrode positive (DCEP), following the procedure previously established by Dalcin et al. [ 7 ]. The geometry and dimensions of the welded joints are schematically illustrated in Fig.  1 , comprising flush-filled flare-bevel groove welds in the longitudinal joints and fillet welds in the transverse joints. The flare-bevel groove welds were produced by machining chamfers on the mating surfaces of the SHS members, reducing the root opening in the curved contact regions and promoting improved weld penetration and fusion. Fig. 1 Geometry of the SHS column-to-beam connection showing the flare-bevel groove welds in the longitudinal joints and fillet welds in the transverse joints. The joint was fabricated using four separate weld beads (two longitudinal and two transverse), resulting in a fully welded perimeter. Weld start and stop locations were positioned approximately 10 mm away from the SHS corner regions

Undermatching (AWS ER80S-G) and overmatching (AWS ER120S-G) solid filler metal with a nominal diameter of 1.2 mm were employed. The beam-to-column connections were fabricated using four separate welds rather than a continuous weld around the SHS perimeter. To avoid weld initiation and termination in the highly constrained corner regions, the start and stop locations of each weld bead were positioned approximately 10 mm away from the SHS corners. For all specimens, a fixed welding sequence was adopted, consisting of the upper transverse weld, lower transverse weld, left longitudinal weld, and right longitudinal weld. This procedure ensured repeatability of weld geometry and thermal cycles throughout the experimental program.

Welding was performed in an automated mode using a  Digiplus A7 450  power source ( IMC - Soldagem ) integrated with a  Tartílope V4  robotic system  (SPS) . All weld beads were deposited using a work angle and travel angle of 0°, with a constant wire stick-out of 20 mm measured from the contact tip. A shielding gas mixture composed of 75 vol.% Ar and 25 vol.% CO₂ was supplied at a flow rate of 15 L/min.

The welding parameters adopted are presented in Table  3  and were continuously monitored using a  SAP - V 4.01  data acquisition system ( IMC - Soldagem ) operating at a sampling frequency of 5 kHz. Weld dimensions were established in accordance with AWS D1.1 [ 31 ]. The effective weld throat was subsequently determined from macrographic measurements and subsequently calculating the effective weld area, which was adopted in the analytical assessment of the joint load-carrying capacity.
 Table 3 Welding conditions for SHS column-to-beam connections Heat input (kJ/mm) Voltage (V) Current (A) Welding speed (mm/s) Wire feed speed (m/min) 0.3 22.0 ± 0.5 141.0 ± 1.5 9.2 4.0 0.6 144.9 ± 2.3 5.0 0.9 148.8 ± 2.8 3.5 1.2 137.3 ± 2.2 2.5 3.7 1.4 129.2 ± 3.0 2.0 3.5 1.6 111.8 ± 1.7 1.5 3.2 Voltage and current values are reported as mean ± standard deviation. Heat input values correspond to the nominal experimental conditions and may differ slightly from values recalculated using the rounded parameters shown in the table

Thermal cycles (Δt 8/5 , corresponding to the weld metal cooling time from 800 to 500 °C) were recorded using type S thermocouples manually inserted into the molten weld pool immediately after the passage of the welding arc [ 32 ]. After insertion, the thermocouple tip remained embedded in the solidifying weld metal, allowing continuous temperature monitoring during cooling and determination of the Δt 8/5  cooling time. The Δt 8/5  values were determined from these measurements and used as an indicator of welding thermal cycle influence on metallurgical transformations and mechanical properties [ 13 ,  15 ]. Temperature data were acquired using a  Lynx ADS2000  system equipped with two 16-channels modules at a sampling rate of 100 Hz.

sections.heading: Metallographic characterization, hardness measurements, and statistical analysis
paragraphs: Metallographic characterization was carried out on transverse cross-sections extracted from welded joints corresponding to each heat input and filler metal. Specimens were prepared in accordance with ASTM E3 [ 33 ], including sectioning with an abrasive cutting disc, mounting in acrylic resin, grinding with SiC papers (#80 to #1200), and polishing with a 3 μm diamond suspension. The samples were etched with a 2% Nital solution to reveal macrostructural and microstructural features.

Macrophotographs (Fig.  2 ) were obtained using a  ZEISS  stereoscopic microscope ( Axio Lab.A1 ). Weld geometry was quantified using  ImageJ  software, enabling calculation of the effective weld area according to AWS D1.1 [ 31 ], defined as the product of the effective weld throat and effective weld length. Microstructural analyses were carried out using a  ZEISS Axio  optical microscope coupled with a digital imaging system operated via  AxioVision  software. Fig. 2 Welded joint geometry and cross-sectional macrographs of flare-bevel-groove welds filled flush in longitudinal joints and the fillet welds in transverse joints, highlighting the weld metal (WM), heat-affected zone (HAZ), and base metal (BM). The effective weld throat was determined from macrographic measurements in accordance with AWS D1.1 and subsequently used to calculate the effective weld area

For each welding condition, three specimens were evaluated. Welded joints were sectioned at the center of the weld length to obtain representative cross-sections for metallographic characterization and hardness measurements. The values reported in the statistical analyses correspond to the mean ± standard deviation obtained from these three independent specimens.

Vickers microhardness measurements were performed in the WM, coarse-grained heat-affected zone (CGHAZ), and BM using an INSIZE microhardness tester (model  ISH-TDV2000-B ). A load of 500 gf was applied for 10 s in accordance with ASTM E384 [ 34 ], allowing assessment of local mechanical property gradients induced by welding thermal cycles. Five independent indentations were performed in each region, and the reported hardness values correspond to the arithmetic means of these measurements. The error bars shown in Fig.  6  represent the corresponding standard deviation.

Microhardness measurements within the HAZ were intentionally concentrated in the CGHAZ, since this region exhibited the most pronounced microstructural modification and could be consistently identified in all welding conditions. Although hardness traverses across all HAZ sub-regions were not performed, the CGHAZ provided a reproducible location for comparative assessment of heat-input-induced property variations.

The influence of heat input and filler metal type (undermatching or overmatching) on WM hardness, HAZ hardness, and stress-resistant section area was statistically evaluated by two-way ANOVA using  MINITAB 16  software, followed by Tukey’s post hoc test [ 35 ]. Statistical significance was assessed at a 95% confidence level ( α  = 0.05). Interaction plots were generated to illustrate combined effects of the investigated factors.

The ANOVA tables report the sum of squares (SS), degrees of freedom (DF), mean square (MS),  F -statistic ( F -value ), and  P -value  for each factor and interaction term. The  F -value  represents the ratio between the variance explained by a factor and the residual variance and was used to assess statistical significance. The Error term represents the unexplained residual variability within the experimental dataset, whereas the Corrected Total corresponds to the total variability after correction for the overall mean.

sections.heading: Static bending test methodology
paragraphs: The static bending behavior of the welded SHS column-to-beam connections was evaluated using a dedicated test bench equipped with an automated hydraulic loading system and a rigid fixation device, as described by Dalcin et al. [ 7 ]. The column was rigidly clamped to prevent translational and rotational motion, while the bending load was applied vertically at the free end of the beam through a rigid loading device, as illustrated in Fig.  3 . A constant displacement rate of 0.2 mm/s was adopted, and tests were conducted until complete structural failure. Selected specimens were subsequently examined by stereoscopic microscopy to characterize fracture locations and surface features after testing. Fig. 3 Schematic representation of the experimental setup used for static bending tests, showing the loading configuration and the positions of the strain gauges

Data acquisition was performed using an  HBM Spider 8  multichannel system, with signals recorded via  Catman 4.5  software at a sampling frequency of 50 Hz. The applied load was measured using a load cell configured in a full Wheatstone bridge, while beam displacement was monitored by a linear variable differential transformer (LVDT) arranged in a half Wheatstone bridge. Strain measurements were obtained using uniaxial and triaxial strain gauges positioned 30 mm from the column face. All strain gauges were connected using a three-wire configuration in a quarter Wheatstone bridge circuit.

sections.heading: Analytical assessment of load-carrying capacity
paragraphs: The ultimate load-carrying capacity of beams with standard geometric proportions is primarily governed by the maximum bending moment sustained prior to failure [ 3 ,  7 ]. For ductile metallic materials subjected to quasi-static loading, structural failure is typically associated with excessive plastic deformation rather than brittle fracture [ 36 ]. When the cross-section thickness is sufficient to prevent local buckling, the ultimate bending moment corresponds to the development of a fully plastic stress distribution, which exceeds the elastic bending moment required to initiate yielding at the outer fibers [ 37 ].

In these expressions,  M  denotes the applied bending moment,  c  the distance from the neutral axis,  I  the second moment of area,  V  the shear force,  Q  the first moment of area of the portion of the cross-section above the point of interest, and  t  the wall thickness. Normal bending stresses vary linearly through the section depth and reach their maximum at the outer fibers, whereas shear stresses are distributed over the cross-section and attain their maximum value at the neutral axis (Fig.  4 ).

The analytical ultimate moment was calculated adopting the lower yield stress between the BM and the WM as the governing criterion (Table  2 ). Because local HAZ mechanical properties were not available, the analytical model assumes homogeneous material behavior and adopts the lower yield stress between the base metal and weld metal as a conservative estimate. Subsequently, the analytical ultimate load was calculated by considering a lever arm of 560 mm, corresponding to the distance between the applied load and the analyzed section at the weld joint (Fig.  3 ).

From a structural integrity perspective, mechanical compatibility between the filler metal and the BM is as critical as the applied heat input in governing joint performance [ 13 ,  18 ]. To account for uncertainties associated with analytical idealizations, manufacturing imperfections, material variability, and long-term degradation mechanisms, allowable stress levels are commonly defined through the application of safety factors in engineering design [ 20 ,  21 ,  38 ]. In the present study, the analytical framework is used primarily for comparative assessment and interpretation rather than for direct design verification.

sections.heading: Finite element modeling and numerical simulation procedure
paragraphs: The welded column-to-beam structure illustrated in Fig.  5  was modeled in three dimensions using SolidWorks® and subsequently imported into Abaqus/CAE® for finite element analysis (FEA). The numerical model represents a cantilever configuration, in which the vertical square hollow section (SHS) column was fully constrained at its base, preventing translations and rotations in all directions to reproduce the rigid boundary conditions adopted in the experimental tests. A vertical concentrated load was applied at the free end of the horizontal beam through a rigid loading device positioned 560 mm from the column face, consistent with the experimental setup shown in Fig.  3 . Numerical simulations were restricted to the optimal heat input condition because this configuration exhibited the highest experimental bending performance and allowed a direct assessment of the effect of filler metal strength mismatch on the structural response. Fig. 5 Finite element model and boundary conditions of the SHS welded joint. The column was fully fixed, and a vertical concentrated load was applied at the free end of the beam

The finite element models were developed for the joints produced with the optimal heat input condition (1.2 kJ/mm). Two configurations were analyzed, corresponding to the undermatching and overmatching filler metals. The welded joints were explicitly modeled as solid volumes, with geometric dimensions defined from macrographic measurements of the corresponding weld beads and according to the geometry illustrated in Fig.  1 . This approach allowed an accurate representation of the weld geometry and ensured consistency between the numerical and experimental configurations. The base metal and weld metal were modeled as isotropic elastoplastic materials with bilinear hardening behavior according to the experimentally materials properties (Table  2 ). The Young’s modulus was taken as 205 GPa for the Strenx®700MC base metal, 210 GPa for the AWS ER120S-G overmatching filler wire, and 200 GPa for the AWS ER80S-G undermatching filler wire, while a Poisson’s ratio of 0.30 was adopted for all materials.

The finite element mesh was generated using first-order tetrahedral solid elements, which capture the complex geometries of the welded joints. Mesh refinement was applied in the weld metal and adjacent regions to accurately 1.5 mm in the weld metal and 3.0 mm in the remaining structure. The final mesh consisted of 84,784 nodes and 295,144 elements, providing a suitable balance between numerical accuracy and computational efficiency.

The numerical simulations were carried out using a static analysis procedure in Abaqus. Load was applied incrementally allowing the identification of yielding initiation, stress redistribution, and the evolution of plastic zones throughout the loading history. Stress outputs included von Mises equivalent stress, principal stresses, and shear stresses. The numerical results were primarily evaluated at critical locations identified experimentally, especially the weld toe on the tension side of the beam, which was consistently associated with failure initiation and final fracture.

The numerical simulations were intended primarily for qualitative assessment of stress redistribution and plastic strain localization rather than for exact prediction of ultimate load capacity. Because spatially varying mechanical properties within the HAZ were not available, the numerical model did not explicitly account for local strength gradients or welding residual stresses. Therefore, the finite element results should be interpreted primarily in a qualitative and comparative manner, focusing on stress redistribution and plastic strain localization mechanisms rather than on exact prediction of ultimate load-carrying capacity.

sections.heading: Experimental evaluation of static bending performance
Influence of heat input and filler metal type on microstructure, hardness, and weld characteristics
paragraphs: Figure  6  presents the variations in weld metal (WM) area, coarse-grained heat-affected zone (CGHAZ) area, fused base metal (BM) area, dilution, throat, effective weld area, WM cooling time (Δt 8/5 ), and CGHAZ hardness as a function of heat input for joints welded with undermatching and overmatching filler metal. Fig. 6 Effect of heat input on weld geometry (WM area, CGHAZ area, fused BM area, dilution, effective weld throat, effective weld area), WM cooling time (Δt 8/5 ), and CGHAZ-WM hardness in the welded joint. Error bars represent the standard deviation obtained from three independent specimens. Hardness values correspond to the average of five indentations performed in each evaluated region

An increase in heat input promoted a progressive enlargement of the WM area, primarily due to the reduction in welding speed and the associated increase in deposited material. The fused BM area increased with heat input up to 1.4 kJ/mm, after which a marked reduction was observed, despite the higher heat input. This behavior is attributed to the decrease in welding current at the highest heat input levels (Table  3 ), which limits penetration efficiency. In all investigated conditions, flare-bevel groove welds exhibited a larger fused BM than fillet welds, reflecting differences in joint geometry and heat concentration [ 7 ].

Heat input had a pronounced effect on the extent of the CGHAZ. For heat inputs above 0.6 kJ/mm, fillet welds exhibited a wider CGHAZ than flare-bevel-groove welds, which is associated with the reduced heat dissipation capability of the 3-mm-thick plates and the more distributed thermal field in fillet weld configurations. Conversely, flare-bevel-groove welds promote deeper but narrower CGHAZ regions due to more localized heat input. These observations highlight the strong coupling between joint geometry and welding thermal cycles. Similar trends have been reported for welded TMCP steels in previous studies [ 7 ,  39 ].

The WM cooling time (Δt 8/5 ) increased progressively with heat input, indicating a reduction in cooling rate and a greater thermal exposure of the welded joint. Concurrently, a systematic decrease in CGHAZ hardness was observed, demonstrating the increasing severity of the welding thermal cycle. The results also show that larger heat inputs promoted greater effective weld areas due to enhanced weld penetration and increased deposited material.

Representative macrographs and microstructures of the welded joints are shown in Fig.  7 a–f. The BM (Fig.  7 f) exhibited a refined ferritic-pearlitic microstructure typical of TMCP steels, characterized by elongated grains inherited from thermomechanical controlled processing [ 1 ,  6 ]. This observation is consistent with previous reports for Strenx®700MC steel [ 40 ]. In addition to grain refinement, the strength of this steel is enhanced by precipitation hardening associated with microalloying elements such as Ti and V [ 41 ,  42 ]. Fig. 7 a  Macrostructure of the flare-bevel groove welds joint produced using AWS ER120S-G filler metal at a heat input of 0.6 kJ/mm. Microstructures of  b  weld metal (WM),  c  coarse grained HAZ (CGHAZ),  d  fine grained HAZ (FGHAZ),  e  intercritical HAZ (ICHAZ), and  f  base metal (BM)

The WM region (Fig.  7 b) presents a bainitic-ferritic microstructure [ 40 ], whereas the HAZ (Fig.  7 c–e) is characterized by pronounced microstructural heterogeneity resulting from the steep thermal gradients imposed during welding [ 29 ,  40 ,  41 ,  43 ]. The CGHAZ is marked by grain coarsening caused by exposure to high peak temperatures, whereas the FGHAZ exhibits a refined transformed microstructure [ 15 ,  40 ]. The ICHAZ is characterized by partial austenitization during the welding thermal cycle followed by transformation during cooling [ 44 ,  45 ]. Although optical microscopy confirms the existence of distinct HAZ sub-regions, detailed phase identification and quantification were beyond the scope of the present study.

The microhardness measurements revealed a progressive reduction in CGHAZ hardness with increasing heat input (Fig.  6 ). In contrast, the WM hardness remained consistently higher than the HAZ hardness for both filler metals. The ANOVA results presented in Table  5  indicate that heat input significantly affected WM hardness, HAZ hardness, and effective weld area ( P  < 0.05). Filler metal type significantly influenced WM hardness and effective weld area, whereas its effect on HAZ hardness was not statistically significant ( P  > 0.05).

Although the trends in effective weld area with increasing heat input were similar for both filler metals, small but systematic differences in weld geometry were observed between the consumables, resulting in a statistically significant filler metal effect. Interaction effects were significant only for the effective weld area. The ANOVA results support experimental observations and demonstrate that heat input is the dominant processing variable affecting HAZ hardness, whereas filler metal type has no statistically significant influence on HAZ softening.

sections.heading: Influence of heat input and filler metal mismatch on static bending performance
paragraphs: Figure  8  presents the experimental load–displacement, moment–rotation, and normal stress–strain relationships obtained for the welded SHS column-to-beam connections. The results show that, for both undermatching and overmatching filler metals, the ultimate bending load increased progressively with heat input up to 1.2 kJ/mm, followed by a reduction at higher heat inputs [ 7 ]. Fig. 8 Experimental bending response of full-scale welded SHS beam-column connections: load–displacement, moment–rotation, and normal stress–strain relationships

The initial increase in load-carrying capacity with heat input is primarily attributed to improved weld penetration and the associated enlargement of the effective weld area [ 7 ]. In this range, the geometric benefits derived from increased weld throat and fused BM area outweigh the metallurgical degradation induced by the thermal cycle. Similar behavior has been reported for welded TMCP steels subjected to moderate heat inputs [ 15 ]. Conversely, at heat inputs above 1.2 kJ/mm, further increases in deposited heat no longer enhance the effective weld area and instead intensify HAZ softening and expansion. Although HAZ softening is already present at lower heat inputs, its influence becomes progressively more significant and eventually outweighs the geometric benefits associated with larger weld dimensions.

At the optimal heat input of 1.2 kJ/mm, the ultimate bending load increased by approximately 31% and 47% compared to joints welded with 0.3 kJ/mm, using overmatching and undermatching filler metals, respectively. Despite the nominal tensile strength of the overmatching filler metal being approximately 44% higher than that of the undermatching filler metal, the difference in ultimate load between the two joint configurations at this optimal condition (1.2 kJ/mm) was limited to approximately 3%, despite the approximately 44% increase in nominal filler metal tensile strength. This result suggests a limited structural effectiveness of overmatching filler metal when failure is governed by HAZ degradation rather than WM yielding. This result indicates that, under bending-dominated loading, global joint resistance is not governed by nominal filler metal tensile strength alone.

The superior local stress capacity of the overmatching filler metal is indicated by the higher WM hardness values shown in Fig.  6 , which serve as an indirect measure of the higher local yield and tensile strength of the WM rather than a direct indicator of structural performance. However, since the effective weld area and the stress field in the BM and HAZ are comparable for both filler metals, the structural response is primarily controlled by the weakest region of the joint, namely the softened HAZ. Figure  6  shows a progressive reduction in HAZ hardness with increasing heat input, while Fig.  8  indicates a corresponding reduction in ultimate load at the highest heat inputs. These results suggest that thermal-cycle-induced softening and local property variations within the HAZ may contribute to plastic stress localization and may influence the ultimate bending capacity regardless of filler metal strength. Similar observations have been reported in welded TMCP steels [ 13 ,  15 ,  16 ].

The HAZ softening observed at higher heat inputs is consistent with thermal-cycle-induced degradation of the TMCP microstructure and the consequent reduction in strengthening mechanisms. In addition, localized grain coarsening and intercritical transformations contribute to the reduction of hardness. Consequently, the HAZ may become one of the mechanically weakest regions of the welded joint, promoting plastic strain localization during bending loading.

Load–displacement curves shown in Fig.  9 a exhibit a nonlinear response characterized by an initial elastic region followed by progressive plastic deformation up to the ultimate load [ 5 ], after which abrupt load drops indicate fracture initiation, as illustrated in Fig.  11 . The corresponding moment–rotation relationships (Fig.  9 b) reveal a semi-rigid joint behavior [ 20 ], with significant moment transfer accompanied by measurable rotation [ 3 ]. This behavior highlights the importance of accounting for joint ductility and rotational capacity in structural design, particularly for welded connections in high-strength TMCP steels. Fig. 9 Effects of filler metal strength and heat input on the static bending behavior of welded connections. ( a ) AWS ER80S-G filler metal, ( b ) AWS ER120S-G filler metal. ( i ) Load versus displacement, ( ii ) Moment (M) versus rotation angle (θ)

Strain gauges measurements (Fig.  10 a, b and Fig.  8 ) confirm that normal bending stresses dominate the mechanical response [ 5 ], where shear stresses remain comparatively low under the adopted cantilever configuration [ 7 ]. Maximum stress consistently occurs at the weld toe on the tension side of the beam, which coincides with the experimentally observed fracture locations (Fig.  11 ). These results indicate that failure initiation is strongly influenced by bending-induced normal stresses acting on regions affected by HAZ softening, rather than by shear or filler metal strength limitations. Fig. 10 Experimental distributions of normal and shear stresses and strains in full-scale welded square hollow sections (SHS) structures: ( a ) AWS ER80S-G filler metal, ( b ) AWS ER120S-G filler metal. ( i ) normal and shear stresses, ( ii ) normal and shear strains Fig. 11 Representative photographs of welded SHS connections produced with a heat input of 1.2 kJ/mm, showing fracture initiation at the weld toe on the tension side of the beam adjacent to the softened HAZ

Representative fracture surface photographs of welded joints produced with a heat input of 1.2 kJ/mm, and macrophotographs correspond to flare-bevel groove welds and fillet welds are shown in Fig.  11 . All welded joints exhibited a ductile fracture behavior, as evidenced by significant plastic deformation and pronounced reduction in cross-sectional area prior to final failure. Although flare-bevel groove welds and fillet welds displayed distinct fracture morphologies due to differences in joint geometry and local stress states, fracture consistently initiated in similar relative regions for a given joint configuration. This observation indicates that failure is governed by localized stress concentration and metallurgical condition rather than geometric differences alone.

For flare-bevel groove welds produced with higher heat inputs, fracture typically initiated in regions adjacent to the weld toe affected by welding thermal cycles, where local softening and stress concentration may have contributed to plastic strain localization (Figs.  6  and  11 ). This behavior reflects the metallurgical degradation induced by prolonged thermal cycles. In TMCP steels such as Strenx®700MC, prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures likely promotes recovery of the deformation-induced dislocation substructure together with coarsening and partial dissolution of Nb(C,N), TiN, and V(C,N) precipitates responsible for precipitation strengthening. Simultaneously, grain coarsening occurs within the CGHAZ. These microstructural changes reduce the effectiveness of grain refinement and precipitation strengthening mechanisms, resulting in localized HAZ softening and increased susceptibility to plastic strain localization under bending-dominated loading.

In contrast, joints welded with lower heat inputs exhibited greater variability in fracture locations among specimens [ 7 ]. No consistent fracture path was identified for these conditions. In fillet welds, higher heat inputs generally lead to fracture initiation along the weld root and toe regions, where stress concentration is more pronounced. Similarly to flare-bevel groove welds, fillet welds produced with low heat inputs exhibited highly scattered and unstable fracture modes, with no consistent fracture location, further highlighting the sensitivity of joint integrity to welding thermal cycles.

These results demonstrate that meeting conventional toughness and ductility requirements for BM and filler metals alone is insufficient to ensure reliable structural performance of welded TMCP steel connections [ 46 ]. Such properties do not fully capture the complex stress states and localized strain concentrations experienced by welded joints under service loading. Therefore, joint-level ductility, stress redistribution capability, and the avoidance of excessively rigid designs must be explicitly considered during welding procedure development and structural design [ 38 ], in agreement with observations reported by Dalcin et al. [ 7 ], who showed that failure initiation in welded SHS connections under bending is associated with the combined effects of weld-toe stress concentration and thermal-cycle-induced property gradients adjacent to the weld, which promote plastic strain localization and crack initiation.

sections.heading: Analytical assessment of load-carrying capacity
paragraphs:
Table  6  compares the experimentally measured ultimate loads with the analytically predicted loads for the investigated welded SHS column-to-beam connections. The analytical assessment was based on classical beam theory combined with welded joint design formulations, assuming elastic–plastic material behavior, uniform material properties, and idealized weld geometries, as described in Sect.  2.2 . The calculated stresses distributions and corresponding strain measurements (Figs.  8  and  10 ) confirmed that the structural response was predominantly governed by bending stresses, with maximum tensile stresses occurring at the weld toe on the tension side of the beam, coinciding with the experimentally observed fracture initiation locations (Fig.  11 ).

The analytically predicted yield loads reported in Table  6  were calculated using Eq. ( 6 ) for the heat input condition of 1.2 kJ/mm, which exhibited the highest experimental load-carrying capacity and was therefore selected as the reference condition for comparison with the finite element simulations presented in Sect.  3.3 . The analytically predicted yield loads reproduced the general trend (Table  6 ), including the increase in load-carrying capacity associated with the enlargement of the effective weld area and the comparatively small structural benefit provided by the overmatching filler metal. However, deviations between analytical and experimental results highlight the limitations of the analytical approach. The model assumes homogeneous mechanical properties and therefore cannot account for thermal-cycle-induced property gradients, localized HAZ softening, or stress redistribution mechanisms associated with plastic strain localization. Consequently, failure is predicted based on global load-carrying capacity without explicitly representing the local degradation phenomena experimentally observed adjacent to the weld toe.

These limitations indicate that analytical formulations are useful for preliminary assessment and comparative interpretation but are insufficient to fully describe the failure behavior of welded TMCP HSLA steel joints. The combination of full-scale experiments and finite element simulations therefore provides a more realistic framework for evaluating the structural performance of welded SHS connections subjected to bending-dominated loading.

sections.heading: Finite element modeling, stress distribution, yielding evolution, and plastic strain localization
paragraphs: Figures  12 ,  13 , and  14  present the numerical results obtained for the welded SHS connections subjected to static bending under optimal heat input condition (1.2 kJ/mm). Fig. 12 von Mises stress distribution from finite element analysis of welded SHS connections under static bending at 50 kN. The overmatching filler metal (AWS ER120S-G) sustains higher local stress levels before extensive yielding develops (> 810 MPa), whereas the more ductile undermatching filler metal (AWS ER80S-G) is limited to approximately 600 MPa due to earlier plastic yielding

Figure  12  shows the von Mises equivalent stress distribution for joints produced with undermatching and overmatching filler metal. In both cases, the highest stress levels are concentrated near the lower weld toe on the tension side of the beam, indicating that this region experiences the most severe loading condition under static bending. The predicted stress concentration location is consistent with the regions where crack initiation was experimentally observed.

The overall stress distribution in the BM is similar for both configurations because identical BM properties were adopted in the simulations [ 7 ]. Differences are mainly restricted to the WM, where the overmatching filler metal sustains higher equivalent stress levels before yielding owing to its higher yield strength (810 MPa). In contrast, the undermatching filler metal reaches its yielding condition at lower stress levels (540 MPa), promoting earlier plastic deformation.

At an applied load of 50 kN, stress values in critical regions approach the nominal tensile strength of the BM. Although this load is reasonably close to the experimentally measured ultimate load (42.0 kN), quantitative agreement should be interpreted with caution because several local phenomena were not explicitly represented in the model.

Figure  13  illustrates the evolution of the equivalent stress field during incremental loading. Yielding initiates earlier in the joint welded with the AWS ER80S-G undermatching filler metal, where a plastic flow begins at a normalized load of approximately 0.175 (≈8.75 kN). In contrast, yielding in the joint welded with the AWS ER120S-G overmatching filler metal starts at approximately 0.25 (≈12.5 kN). This difference is directly associated with the lower yield strength of the undermatching filler metal. Fig. 13 Evolution of von Mises stress in welded joints with undermatching and overmatching filler metal, showing stress concentration at the weld toe on the tension side of the beam. The undermatching filler metal (AWS ER80S-G) exhibits earlier yielding and a more extensive plastic zone development compared with the overmatching filler metal (AWS ER120S-G). The same color scale was used for all loading conditions and filler metal type to enable direct comparison of stress evolution

As the applied load increases, the plastified region expands from the highly stressed geometric discontinuities toward adjacent portions of the joint. The undermatching filler metal develops a larger plastic zone throughout the loading history, while the overmatching weld exhibits a more confined plastified region. Consequently, overmatching filler metal delays yielding but does not substantially alter the location of the most critical stress concentration region. These results indicate that filler metal strength primarily affects the onset and extent of yielding within the WM rather than the global stress distribution of the welded connection.

The equivalent plastic strain distributions presented in Fig.  14  show that the highest levels of accumulated plastic deformation occur in regions adjacent to the lower weld toe for both filler metal types. Although the magnitude and spatial extent of the plastic zone differ between the two filler metal, the location of maximum plastic strain remains essentially unchanged. The undermatching filler metal develops a broader plastified region, promoting earlier stress redistribution, whereas the overmatching filler metal concentrates higher stresses before yielding. Fig. 14 Equivalent plastic strain distributions from finite element simulations, showing localized plastic deformation at the weld toe and adjacent regions where HAZ softening was experimentally identified for undermatching (AWS ER80S-G) and overmatching (AWS ER120S-G) filler metal

The regions exhibiting elevated plastic strain coincided with the locations where reduced hardness and crack initiation were experimentally identified. This spatial correspondence indicates that the finite element predictions are consistent with the experimentally identified critical regions. However, because the model did not explicitly incorporate spatial variations in HAZ properties, the numerical results should be interpreted as qualitative support for the experimental observations rather than as direct evidence of a causal relationship. The numerical simulations were developed primarily to identify stress concentration regions, yielding evolution, and plastic strain localization mechanisms. Several factors known to influence the mechanical response of welded joints were not explicitly included in the model, which include the following: The explicit representation of individual HAZ sub-regions Welding residual stresses Spatial gradients of mechanical properties produced by welding thermal cycles.

Consequently, the simulations should be interpreted as a qualitative and comparative assessment of the influence of filler metal mismatch rather than as a rigorous prediction of ultimate load-carrying capacity. Nevertheless, the numerical results successfully reproduced the experimentally observed critical regions and provided useful insight into the stress redistribution and plastic deformation mechanisms governing the structural response of the welded SHS connections.

Although hardness measurements and fracture observations consistently indicate an association between HAZ softening and failure initiation, a detailed characterization of the individual HAZ sub-regions (ICHAZ and SCHAZ), continuous hardness mapping, and incorporation of local HAZ properties into the finite element model were beyond the scope of the present study. Therefore, the proposed failure mechanism should be interpreted as strongly supported by the available experimental evidence but not as a direct demonstration of causality.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The present results demonstrate that the static bending performance of welded SHS column-to-beam connections manufactured from Strenx®700MC steel is controlled by the interaction between weld geometry and thermal-cycle-induced microstructural degradation. Although the experimental results were presented as a function of nominal heat input, the governing metallurgical variables are the thermal cycle characteristics, particularly the WM cooling time (Δt 8/5 ) and the residence time of the HAZ above the austenitization and/or recrystallization temperatures [ 6 ,  47 ]. These parameters strongly influence grain growth, recovery process, and precipitation-strengthening mechanisms that govern the local hardness and strength of TMCP steels [ 6 ,  13 ,  15 ,  47 ]. Therefore, heat input should be interpreted as an indicator of thermal-cycle severity rather than as the fundamental metallurgical variable [ 7 ,  15 ,  16 ].

The progressive reduction in CGHAZ hardness observed with increasing heat input is consistent with the metallurgical behavior of Strenx®700MC and other TMCP HSLA steels. Strength in these materials is primarily derived from grain refinement and precipitation strengthening mechanisms, both of which are highly sensitive to thermal exposure during welding [ 13 ,  15 ,  16 ]. Increasing thermal-cycle severity promotes recovery of the deformation-induced dislocation structure and coarsening or partial dissolution of Nb(C,N), TiN, and V(C,N) precipitates, reducing the effectiveness of precipitation hardening [ 41 ,  42 ]. Although hardness measurements in the present study were limited to the CGHAZ, the observed trends are consistent with previous investigations reporting softening within HAZ sub-regions reported in welded TMCP steels [ 13 ].

The statistical analysis further reinforces this interpretation. The ANOVA results demonstrate that heat input is the dominant factor affecting HAZ hardness, WM hardness, and effective weld area, whereas nominal filler metal tensile strength plays a comparatively secondary role. Heat input was statistically significant ( P -value  < 0.05) for all responses investigated and represented the dominant factor affecting the observed variability. In contrast, filler metal strength did not significantly affect HAZ hardness ( P -value  > 0.05), despite its influence on WM hardness. Since HAZ softening and thermal-cycle-induced property gradients contribute to plastic strain localization and failure initiation, these findings indicate that thermal-cycle effects have a greater influence on structural performance than by nominal filler metal tensile strength mismatch. Furthermore, a significant interaction between heat input and filler metal strength was observed only for the effective weld area ( P -value  < 0.05), whereas no significant interaction was detected for WM and HAZ hardness ( P -value  > 0.05). Collectively, these results quantitatively support the conclusion that heat input, through its influence on weld geometry and HAZ softening, is the primary processing parameter controlling the bending performance of Strenx®700MC welded SHS connections.

The results further indicate that the beneficial effect of increasing heat input is limited. At low and intermediate heat inputs, improved penetration and enlargement of the effective weld area enhance load transfer and increase joint resistance. However, as thermal-cycle severity increases, the resulting HAZ softening progressively offsets these geometric benefits [ 7 ,  13 ,  18 ,  39 ]. Consequently, the optimum performance observed near 1.2 kJ/mm appears to result from a balance between geometric efficiency and thermal-cycle-induced degradation.

An important outcome of this study is the limited structural benefit provided by overmatching filler metal. Increasing the nominal filler metal tensile strength mismatch by approximately 44% produced only a 3% increase in ultimate bending capacity. Numerical simulations showed that overmatching delayed WM yielding but did not significantly alter the stress concentration regions or locations of plastic strain localization. These observations suggest that, under bending-dominated loading, the structural response is more strongly influenced by thermal-cycle-induced property gradients adjacent to the weld than by nominal filler metal tensile strength alone [ 26 ,  28 ,  30 ].

This behavior is consistent with previous studies on welded TMCP steels [ 13 ,  15 ], which have reported that welding thermal cycles exert a stronger influence on local mechanical properties than by nominal filler metal tensile strength mismatch. The present work extends these observations by demonstrating the same trend at the structural scale through the combination of full-scale testing, statistical analysis, analytical assessment, and finite element simulations.

From an engineering perspective, the findings indicate that welding procedure development for TMCP HSLA steels should prioritize thermal-cycle control rather than the indiscriminate use of excessively overmatching filler metal. While overmatching filler metal may remain beneficial when WM yielding controls structural performance, their effectiveness becomes limited when failure initiation is associated with thermal-cycle-induced degradation in the HAZ [ 18 ,  39 ]. Therefore, controlling Δt 8/5  and minimizing excessive thermal exposure appear to be more effective strategies for improving the structural performance and reliability of welded SHS connections [ 7 ,  18 ,  39 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Heat input was identified as the dominant factor controlling HAZ softening in GMAW-welded Strenx®700MC SHS column-to-beam connections. ANOVA results confirmed a statistically significant effect of heat input on HAZ hardness ( P  < 0.001), whereas filler metal type showed no significant influence ( P  = 0.49). An optimal heat input of approximately 1.2 kJ/mm was identified. Below this level, increased weld penetration and effective weld area enhanced load-carrying capacity, whereas higher heat inputs promote HAZ degradation that offset these geometric benefits. Increasing nominal filler metal tensile strength by approximately 44% through overmatching resulted in only a 3% increase in ultimate bending load, demonstrating the limited structural effectiveness of WM overmatching under bending-dominated loading. Experimental observations, analytical calculations, and finite element simulations consistently identified the weld toe and adjacent HAZ region as the most critical locations associated with stress concentration, plastic strain accumulation, and fracture initiation. For welded Strenx®700MC SHS beam-to-column connections, optimization of the welding thermal cycle is more effective than WM overmatching for improving structural performance. Consequently, welding procedure development for TMCP high-strength steels should prioritize thermal-cycle control rather than the indiscriminate use of overmatching filler metal.
